one_liner: Header-only functional helpers (keep_if, transform, fold, compose) over STL containers; matches std::copy_if speed, does not beat it.
what_it_does: FunctionalPlus wraps common loops as pure functions that take and return ordinary STL containers: fplus::keep_if(pred, xs) returns a new filtered container instead of writing through an output iterator, and fplus::fwd:: offers curried versions for pipe-style chaining with fwd::apply and fwd::compose. It is a different interface from <algorithm>, not a drop-in: results are returned by value and whole containers are passed instead of iterator pairs. The library also carries maybe/result types, string tools, a tree type, timing helpers and parallel transforms.
how_it_is_fast: It is not faster; it aims for zero overhead over the STL. keep_if on a const lvalue is literally std::copy_if into std::back_inserter on a fresh container (filter.hpp, create_new_container_t path), so it compiles to the same code as the baseline. When the argument is a non-const r-value (e.g. in chained calls) it dispatches on internal::can_reuse_v and filters in place with the erase-remove idiom, saving one allocation and copy per stage.
when_to_use: Readability-first code that filters, maps and folds std::vector/std::list/std::string and wants value-returning functions instead of output iterators.
Chained transformations where intermediate containers are r-values, so keep_if/sort/transform can reuse the input buffer in place.
C++14 codebases that cannot move to C++20 std::ranges but want composable container operations.
Prototyping data-processing code where a later profiling pass replaces only the hot stages with hand-written loops.
when_not_to_use: When you need a speedup over std::copy_if or a hand loop: the only published measurement is parity, and the code path is std::copy_if itself.
Long pipelines on large inputs where materialising every intermediate container costs memory and bandwidth; lazy std::ranges or range-v3 views allocate nothing between stages (README).
Hot paths that call the more complex functions; the README says some of them could be written more efficiently and invites reports.

Build-time-sensitive projects: the umbrella header (the all-in-one fplus.hpp is about 16,100 lines, 565 KB) includes 43 distinct standard headers (iostream, fstream, future, thread, map, random among them), and the CMake target links Threads::Threads.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime; CMake target requires Threads (find_package(Threads REQUIRED)); Python optional to regenerate fwd/curry headers
integration.min_toolchain: C++14; GCC 4.9+, Clang 3.7+ with libc++ 3.7+, Visual Studio 2015+, Xcode 9+
integration.platforms: any platform with a C++14 compiler and the standard library
integration.thread_safety: Functions are pure over their arguments; transform_parallelly uses std::async and transform_parallelly_n_threads std::thread; benchmark_session guards its map with a std::mutex. No broader thread-safety statement is documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — keep_if(pred, xs) replaces a copy_if-into-back_inserter idiom on a whole container, but it is not an iterator-based algorithm and always returns a new (or reused r-value) container

gotchas: Harness flaw: the README numbers come from examples/readme_perf_examples.cpp, which is public (the record's claim that no benchmark code is in the repo is wrong). In it fplus::keep_if receives a const lvalue, so it runs exactly std::copy_if with std::back_inserter; the 0.641 s vs 0.627 s gap is run-to-run noise between identical code, not a library effect.

The same harness sets numRuns = 10 when NDEBUG is defined (the '#if defined NDEBUG || defined _DEBUG' guard is inverted relative to its 'make debug runs faster' comment), so a standard CMake Release build (-O3 -DNDEBUG) times only 10 runs; the README's 20000-run figures need a build without NDEBUG.

Every timed call goes through std::function<std::vector<int>(std::vector<int>)> and copies the 5000-int input by value, an allocation plus 20 KB copy per iteration shared by all three variants, which dilutes any difference; timing uses system_clock, one pass, no spread.
In-place reuse only happens for non-const r-values whose value_type is self-assignable; passing an lvalue silently allocates a new container.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued utilities siblings (micron.cpp memcpy/memset, netbsd-curses) solve unrelated problems; pick FunctionalPlus only for expressive container algorithms at STL speed, not for a measured speedup.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README run of examples/readme_perf_examples.cpp: keeping the odd values of 5000 rand() integers, 20000 runs accumulated, GCC with -O3 on an unnamed desktop PC, gave hand loop 0.632 s, std::copy_if 0.641 s and fplus::keep_if 0.627 s. Because keep_if on that input is std::copy_if, this shows zero abstraction overhead, not a speedup.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-13 adding a Clang 23 CI build, version 0.2.28), BSL-1.0, 2.3k stars, packaged in vcpkg and Conan; copyable, but catalogued as a parity entry with no performance advantage over std::copy_if.
